title: 22. Interview: Partitioning
summary: Interview Q&A for Partitioning — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Partitioning interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What's the difference between partitioning and sharding?
**Answer:** Partitioning and sharding both split data, but at different scopes. Partitioning splits a single logical table into smaller physical partitions **within one database server** — shared CPU, RAM, and disk. It is a storage and query optimization that stays invisible to the deployment topology. Sharding splits data **across multiple independent database servers**, each with its own CPU, RAM, disk, and replicas — it is a horizontal-scaling technique for when one machine cannot hold the data. A partitioned table can still fit on one box; a sharded table cannot. The application code differs: partitioning is transparent (the planner handles pruning automatically), so queries don't change. Sharding requires a shard-aware client or proxy that routes by shard key — non-trivial application changes. The operational models differ: partitioning is one DBA managing one server; sharding is N servers, each with its own failure modes, backups, and replicas. A common pattern is to combine them — each shard is itself partitioned, giving two levels of subdivision. Real-world: PostgreSQL partitioning handles a 5TB table on one server; Cassandra's "partitioning" doubles as sharding because each partition is placed on a different node via consistent hashing.
**Visual:**
```
PARTITIONING (1 server):            SHARDING (N servers):
+-------------------------------+   +------+ +------+ +------+
| DB Server                     |   |Shard0| |Shard1| |Shard2|
|  events table                 |   | 1/3  | | 1/3  | | 1/3  |
|   p2023 p2024 p2025           |   | rows | | rows | | rows |
|  (shared CPU/RAM/disk)        |   +------+ +------+ +------+
+-------------------------------+   (independent servers)
transparent to queries             shard-aware client required
```

### Q2. When would you use range vs list vs hash partitioning?
**Answer:** **Range partitioning** is best when the partition key has a natural order and queries filter by range — typically time-series data. Partition `events` by `created_at` into daily or monthly partitions; queries like `WHERE created_at >= '2024-03-01'` prune to one partition. Also enables instant partition drops for retention (`DROP TABLE p2023_01` vs slow DELETE). **List partitioning** is best when the partition key has a small, known set of discrete values and queries filter by exact match. Partition `customers` by `region` (US, EU, Asia) so a query `WHERE region='EU'` hits one partition. Useful for multi-tenant SaaS where each tenant or region is its own partition. **Hash partitioning** is best when the goal is even distribution and there's no natural range or list. Partition `users` by `hash(user_id) % 32` for 32 evenly-sized partitions; queries `WHERE user_id=?` hit one partition. Hash partitioning does NOT support range pruning — `WHERE created_at > X` scatters across all partitions. The choice: use range for time-series with retention needs, list for known discrete categories, hash for even distribution without natural boundaries. Many real systems combine: range-partition by date, then sub-partition each range by hash of user_id. PostgreSQL supports all three; MySQL supports range and list (hash exists but is less flexible).
**Visual:**
```
RANGE (time-series):           LIST (regions):            HASH (even split):
p_2024_01: ts in Jan           p_us:  region='US'         p0..p31: hash(id) % 32
p_2024_02: ts in Feb           p_eu:  region IN(UK,FR,DE) -> 32 even partitions
p_2024_03: ts in Mar           p_asia: region IN(CN,JP,IN) WHERE id=? hits 1 part
WHERE ts >= '2024-03-01'       WHERE region='EU' hits 1   WHERE ts>X scatters (no range)
-> prunes to p_2024_03         (small discrete value set)  (good for equality, not range)
```

### Q3. What is partition pruning and why does it matter?
**Answer:** Partition pruning is the query planner's ability to skip partitions that cannot contain matching rows, based on the WHERE clause. If `events` is partitioned by `created_at` into monthly partitions and the query is `SELECT * FROM events WHERE created_at >= '2024-03-01' AND created_at < '2024-04-01'`, the planner reads the partition catalog, sees that only `p2024_03` overlaps the date range, and scans only that partition. The other 11 partitions are never touched — no I/O, no index lookups, no locking. For a 12-partition table, this is a 12x speedup on average; for a 365-partition table (daily partitions for a year), it can be 365x. Pruning works at **plan time** (static pruning, when the WHERE clause has literal values) or **execution time** (dynamic pruning, when the WHERE clause has parameters — the planner prepares all partitions but skips non-matching ones at runtime based on parameter values). The catch: pruning only works if the WHERE clause includes the partition key. A query `SELECT * FROM events WHERE type='login'` (no `created_at` filter) hits every partition — the planner cannot prune. This is why partition key choice is critical: it must align with the most common query patterns. Real-world: PostgreSQL's EXPLAIN shows "Subplans Removed: N" indicating pruned partitions.
**Visual:**
```
Query: SELECT * FROM events WHERE created_at >= '2024-03-15' AND type='login'

Planner checks partition bounds:
  p2024_01 [Jan 1 - Feb 1)   -- skipped (no overlap)
  p2024_02 [Feb 1 - Mar 1)   -- skipped (no overlap)
  p2024_03 [Mar 1 - Apr 1)   -- SCANNED (overlaps)
  p2024_04 [Apr 1 - May 1)   -- skipped (no overlap)

Result: 1 of 4 partitions scanned = 4x speedup
EXPLAIN: "Subplans Removed: 3"
```

### Q4. How does vertical partitioning differ from horizontal, and when do you use it?
**Answer:** Horizontal partitioning splits a table by **rows** — each partition has the same columns but a subset of rows. Vertical partitioning splits a table by **columns** — each partition has the same rows but a subset of columns. Vertical partitioning is used when one table has many columns and only a few are accessed frequently. For example, a `users` table with 50 columns (id, name, email, password_hash, bio, avatar_url, preferences_json, billing_address, last_50_logins, ...) — 99% of queries only need `id, name, email`. Splitting into `users_core` (10 hot columns, fits in cache) and `users_profile` (40 cold columns, accessed only on profile page) makes the hot queries faster: less I/O per row, more rows per cache page. Vertical partitioning is also useful for isolating columns with different update patterns — a hot column (last_login_at) and a cold column (bio) can be split so updates to the hot column don't rewrite the cold column's data (important for MVCC databases like PostgreSQL that rewrite the whole row on update). Real-world: WhatsApp vertically splits message tables — small hot metadata (sender, timestamp) in one table, large cold media URLs in another. PostgreSQL's TOAST mechanism is automatic vertical partitioning for large columns (over ~2KB stored out-of-line). The trade-off: vertical partitioning makes SELECT * slower (joins across partitions) and complicates schema changes (DDL on multiple tables). Use it only when column access is highly skewed.
**Visual:**
```
HORIZONTAL (split by rows):       VERTICAL (split by columns):
+------------------+              +----------+ +--------------+
| p_2024_01 rows   |              | users_   | | users_       |
| p_2024_02 rows   |              | core:    | | profile:     |
| p_2024_03 rows   |              |  id,name | |  id,bio,     |
| (all columns,    |              |  ,email  | |  avatar,pref |
|  subset of rows) |              | (hot,    | | (cold, 1%    |
+------------------+              |  99% use)| |  of queries) |
                                  +----------+ +--------------+
```

### Q5. How does Cassandra's partition key differ from PostgreSQL partitioning?
**Answer:** In PostgreSQL, partitioning is a **storage optimization** on a single server — the partition key routes rows to local partitions, and the planner prunes them. In Cassandra, the partition key is the **fundamental unit of data distribution and access** — it determines which node stores the data, which nodes replicate it, and which queries are even possible. Every Cassandra table has a partition key (the first part of the PRIMARY KEY). Rows with the same partition key are stored together as a "partition" on one node (and its replicas). A query MUST include the partition key in the WHERE clause — otherwise the coordinator must scatter-gather across all nodes, which is allowed but discouraged (slow, allows hotspotting). Within a partition, rows are sorted by clustering columns (the rest of the PRIMARY KEY), so range scans within a partition are efficient. This means Cassandra's data model forces you to design tables around your queries — you denormalize aggressively so each query hits one partition. PostgreSQL, by contrast, lets you write any SQL query and the planner figures it out. Real-world: Instagram on Cassandra stores `feed` rows keyed by `(user_id, ts)` — fetching a user's feed is one partition read with a range scan on `ts`. You couldn't do this on a "general" table — the schema is the query. The trade-off: Cassandra gives you horizontal scale for free but locks in query patterns; PostgreSQL gives you query flexibility but doesn't scale horizontally without sharding.
**Visual:**
```
PostgreSQL (1 server):            Cassandra (N servers):
events PARTITION BY RANGE (ts)    CREATE TABLE feed (
  p_2024_01, p_2024_02, ...         user_id uuid,
  planner prunes by ts              ts timestamp,
any SQL query allowed               post_id uuid,
                                    PRIMARY KEY (user_id, ts)
                                  );
                                  -> partition key = user_id
                                  -> 1 node owns each partition
                                  query MUST have WHERE user_id=?
```

### Q6. What are the limitations of partitioning?
**Answer:** Partitioning has real limitations. (1) **Partition key must be part of the primary key** in PostgreSQL — if you partition `orders` by `created_at`, the PK is `(id, created_at)`, not just `id`. This breaks ORMs and complicates FK references. (2) **Unique constraints are partition-local** — `UNIQUE(user_id, email)` enforces uniqueness within one partition, not globally. To enforce global uniqueness, use an application-level check or a separate lookup table. (3) **Foreign keys pointing to a partitioned table aren't supported** (PostgreSQL ≤16). You can have FKs FROM a partitioned table TO a regular table, but not the reverse. (4) **Cross-partition queries are slow** — without the partition key in the WHERE clause, the planner scatters across all partitions. (5) **Partition count has overhead** — PostgreSQL planning time degrades past a few thousand partitions; use subpartitioning or partition management tools (pg_partman) for high counts. (6) **Schema changes are amplified** — `ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN` propagates to all partitions; on a 1000-partition table, this is slow and locks. (7) **Updates that change the partition key move the row** — `UPDATE events SET created_at = ...` where the new value falls in a different partition triggers a DELETE + INSERT, which is expensive and can fail if there's no partition for the new value. (8) **No global statistics** — the planner uses per-partition stats, which can produce suboptimal plans for cross-partition queries. The lesson: partitioning is a sharp tool; use it for time-series and large append-only tables, not for OLTP with frequent updates and FKs.
**Visual:**
```
LIMITATIONS:
  PK must include partition key       -> breaks ORMs
  UNIQUE constraint                   -> local only, not global
  FK -> partitioned table             -> not supported (PG <=16)
  Cross-partition query               -> scatter, slow
  >1000 partitions                    -> plan time degrades
  UPDATE changing partition key       -> DELETE+INSERT (expensive)
  ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN              -> propagates to all parts (slow)

Use partitioning for: time-series, logs, events, append-only
Avoid for: small OLTP tables, FK-heavy schemas, frequent updates
```

### Q7. How does partitioning help with data lifecycle (retention, archival)?
**Answer:** Partitioning makes data lifecycle operations O(1) instead of O(N). Without partitioning, deleting old data is `DELETE FROM events WHERE created_at < '2024-01-01'` — a slow operation that scans the table, writes tombstones, holds locks, and then requires a VACUUM to reclaim space (which can take hours on a large table). With partitioning, the equivalent is `DROP TABLE p2023_12` — instantaneous, returns disk immediately, no locks on the rest of the table, no VACUUM. This is why time-series partitioning is the standard pattern for retention: partition by day or month, keep N partitions hot, drop old ones on a schedule. For archival, instead of dropping, you can detach a partition (`ALTER TABLE events DETACH PARTITION p2023_12`) which leaves the data intact as a standalone table — then dump it to Parquet on S3, load it into BigQuery for analytics, and drop the local copy. This pattern is called **tiered storage**: hot data (last 30 days) on fast NVMe in the operational DB, warm data (30-365 days) on cheaper SSD, cold data (1+ years) on S3 or a columnar warehouse. Real-world: PostgreSQL + pg_partman automates this — create partitions ahead of time, drop old ones on a schedule, optionally run a "detached partition → S3" archival step. TimescaleDB and Citus have similar features. The win: a 10-year retention policy is feasible because only the last month's data is in the hot database; everything older is in cold object storage.
**Visual:**
```
RETENTION with partitioning:
  Day 1:  p2024_03_01 ... p2024_03_31 (active)
  Day 32: CREATE p2024_04_01
          DROP p2024_03_01  (instant, returns disk)
          -> no DELETE, no VACUUM, no locks

ARCHIVAL (tiered storage):
  DETACH p2023_12  -> standalone table
  pg_dump -> S3 parquet -> BigQuery
  DROP p2023_12
  -> hot DB stays small, cold data in warehouse
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. You're building a logging system that ingests 1B events/day with a 90-day retention. How do you partition?
**Answer:** I'd partition by day using range partitioning on `ingested_at` — 90 daily partitions hot, with a daily job that creates tomorrow's partition ahead of time and drops the one 91 days old. Schema: `CREATE TABLE events (id bigint, type text, payload jsonb, ingested_at timestamptz NOT NULL) PARTITION BY RANGE (ingested_at);` with each daily partition being `events_YYYY_MM_DD`. I'd use PostgreSQL with pg_partman to automate partition creation and dropping. Each daily partition would have a local BRIN index on `ingested_at` (compact, since the data is naturally ordered) and a local B-tree on `type` for filter queries. Queries like `SELECT count(*) FROM events WHERE ingested_at >= NOW() - INTERVAL '1 day' AND type='error'` prune to one partition and scan its local index. For retention: a daily cron job runs `DROP TABLE events_YYYY_MM_DD` for the partition 91 days old — instant, no VACUUM. For archival: before dropping, optionally `DETACH PARTITION` and dump to S3 Parquet for long-term analytics in BigQuery. The hot database stays at ~90 days × 1B = 90B rows across 90 partitions, each ~1B rows — large but manageable with local indexes. Writes go to today's partition only (hot write target — that's fine, it's expected and bounded). If a single day's writes overwhelm one partition, I'd subpartition by hour or by hash of `id`. This pattern is used by Stripe, Slack, and many SaaS logging systems.
**Visual:**
```
events PARTITION BY RANGE (ingested_at)
  p2024_03_15 (1B rows, today's writes go here)
  p2024_03_16 ... p2024_06_12 (active, 90 days)
  p2024_06_13 (tomorrow, pre-created)

Daily cron:
  1. CREATE p2024_06_14
  2. DROP p2024_03_16 (91 days old, instant)
  3. (optional) DETACH p2024_03_16 -> S3 -> BigQuery before drop

Query: WHERE ingested_at = '2024-04-01' AND type='error'
  -> prunes to p2024_04_01, scans local type index
```

### Q2. A multi-tenant SaaS has 1000 customers with very different sizes — one customer has 50% of the rows. How do you partition?
**Answer:** I would NOT partition by customer_id with hash partitioning — one customer (50% of rows) would make one partition huge and skew every query. Instead, I'd use a **directory-based or list partitioning** approach that puts large customers on their own partitions and groups small customers together. Specifically: partition by `customer_tier` (a column I add): `tier='enterprise_42'` for the big customer (own partition), `tier='enterprise'` for the next 10 largest (one partition each or grouped), `tier='standard'` for the next 100 (grouped), `tier='small'` for the rest (one partition). This gives roughly balanced partitions. For the giant customer, if their partition is still too big, subpartition it by hash of `id` into 8 sub-partitions. Queries by customer_id would need a small lookup table mapping `customer_id -> partition_name` (or just include `customer_tier` in the WHERE clause). A more elegant solution if PostgreSQL is the choice: use **row-level security** with a single table — no partitioning needed; let the planner filter by `customer_id` via indexes. If writes are the bottleneck (the big customer dominates writes), consider moving them to a dedicated database entirely — that's effectively sharding them out. Real-world: Salesforce partitions by customer with this tiered approach; large enterprise tenants get dedicated "pod" databases, small customers share. The principle: don't let one partition dominate; isolate the hot tenant.
**Visual:**
```
BAD: hash(customer_id) % 8
  p0: 500M rows (the giant customer!)  <-- skew
  p1-p7: 50M rows each

GOOD: list partition by tier
  p_enterprise_42: tier='enterprise_42'  (own partition, 500M rows)
    -> subpartition by hash(id) % 8     (8 sub-parts of 62M each)
  p_enterprise: tier='enterprise'       (10 customers, 50M rows)
  p_standard: tier='standard'           (100 customers, 30M rows)
  p_small: tier='small'                 (889 customers, 20M rows)
  -> all partitions roughly balanced
```

### Q3. You have a `users` table with 50 columns; 5 columns (id, name, email, last_login) are accessed 99% of the time. The other 45 columns (bio, avatar, preferences, history) are accessed 1%. How do you optimize?
**Answer:** This is the textbook case for vertical partitioning (or columnar storage). I'd split the `users` table into two: `users_core` (the 5 hot columns, ~50 bytes/row) and `users_profile` (the 45 cold columns, ~5KB/row), joined by `user_id`. The hot table fits entirely in RAM (50 bytes × 100M users = 5GB), so all reads are cache hits — sub-millisecond. The cold table is only touched on profile page loads (1% of traffic), where the extra join cost is acceptable. The benefit: 99% of queries do `SELECT id, name, email FROM users_core WHERE id=?` — a single-table, cache-resident read. Without vertical partitioning, the same query would read a row of ~5KB (50 columns), wasting I/O and cache space on 45 unused columns. In PostgreSQL, this is implemented as two tables with a foreign key from `users_profile.user_id` to `users_core.id`, plus a view `CREATE VIEW users AS SELECT c.*, p.* FROM users_core c LEFT JOIN users_profile p ON c.id = p.user_id` for compatibility. Alternatively, PostgreSQL's TOAST automatically moves large columns (over ~2KB) out of the main row, achieving similar benefits automatically for large columns but not for many small columns. For analytical workloads, a columnar store (Parquet, ClickHouse, Citus columnar) achieves vertical partitioning natively — each column is stored separately, and queries only read the columns they reference. Real-world: WhatsApp vertically splits its message tables — small hot metadata in one table, large media URLs in another.
**Visual:**
```
BEFORE (1 wide table):
  users (id, name, email, last_login, bio, avatar, prefs, ...45 cols)
  row size: ~5KB
  SELECT name FROM users WHERE id=42
    -> reads 5KB to get 50 bytes  (wasteful)

AFTER (vertical partition):
  users_core (id, name, email, last_login)        ~50 bytes/row, in RAM
  users_profile (user_id, bio, avatar, prefs, ...) ~5KB/row, cold

  Hot query: SELECT name FROM users_core WHERE id=42  (50 bytes, cache hit)
  Profile page: SELECT c.*, p.* FROM users_core c
                JOIN users_profile p ON c.id=p.user_id  (rare, OK to be slow)
```

### Q4. You're migrating a 5-year-old PostgreSQL `events` table (3TB, no partitioning) to daily partitioning with no downtime. How?
**Answer:** Migration to partitioning is non-trivial because PostgreSQL doesn't support `ALTER TABLE ... PARTITION BY` on an existing table. The plan: (1) **Create a new partitioned table** `events_new` with the same schema, `PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at)`, and a daily partition for today and the next 30 days. (2) **Set up a trigger on the old table** that mirrors writes to `events_new` (after insert/update/delete) — dual-write via trigger. (3) **Backfill** historical data: a background job copies rows from `events` to `events_new` in chunks by date, oldest to newest, rate-limited to avoid overloading. Use `INSERT INTO events_new SELECT * FROM events WHERE created_at >= '2019-01-01' AND created_at < '2019-02-01'` per month, with `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` to skip rows already mirrored by the trigger. (4) **Verify**: run a checksum comparison between the two tables per date range; fix discrepancies. (5) **Cut over reads**: change the application to read from `events_new`; keep `events` as a fallback. Shadow-read for 24 hours, comparing results. (6) **Rename**: in a single transaction, rename `events` to `events_old` and `events_new` to `events`. (7) **Decommission** `events_old` after a week of stability. Tools like `pg_partman` and `pglogical` can help; citus has a `citus_partition` migration tool. The whole migration takes days to weeks for a 3TB table; the key is incremental backfill with verification.
**Visual:**
```
Phase 1: CREATE events_new PARTITION BY RANGE (ts)
         + today/next 30 days partitions
Phase 2: TRIGGER on events -> mirror to events_new (dual-write)
Phase 3: Backfill (per-month chunks, ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING):
         INSERT INTO events_new SELECT * FROM events
           WHERE ts >= '2019-01' AND ts < '2019-02'
         ... (rate-limited, parallelizable)
Phase 4: Verify (per-range checksum)
Phase 5: Shadow reads (1% -> 100%)
Phase 6: RENAME events -> events_old, events_new -> events
Phase 7: DROP events_old (after 1 week stable)
```

### Q5. A time-series workload has 1M inserts/sec and queries that always filter by `device_id` and `ts` range. Partition by `ts` alone or by `(device_id, ts)`?
**Answer:** I'd partition by `ts` (range, daily) AND subpartition by hash of `device_id` within each day — a two-level scheme. Rationale: the query pattern is `WHERE device_id=? AND ts >= ? AND ts < ?`. The `ts` filter enables partition pruning on the outer range partition (one day). The `device_id` filter is an equality, but if all devices' data for a day is in one partition, the query scans that day's index on `device_id` for the specific device — workable but not optimal. With subpartitioning by `hash(device_id) % 16`, the query prunes to one day AND one device-hash sub-partition — a 1/(days*16) scan, much smaller. The trade-off: more partitions (365 days × 16 = 5840 partitions per year — at PostgreSQL's soft limit, but doable with subpartitioning and pg_partman). Retention is still easy: drop daily partitions (cascades to sub-partitions). Writes: today's 1M inserts/sec spread across 16 sub-partitions = ~62k writes/sec per sub-partition — manageable. An alternative is TimescaleDB's "hypertable" which auto-partitions by time and lets you specify "space partitions" (by `device_id`) — natively supports this two-level scheme with better tooling. Real-world: IoT platforms (InfluxDB, TimescaleDB) use this pattern — partition by time for retention, sub-partition by device for query locality. The key principle: choose partition keys that match the query predicates; both `ts` (for range pruning and retention) and `device_id` (for equality pruning) are needed.
**Visual:**
```
Two-level partitioning:
  events PARTITION BY RANGE (ts)
    p2024_03_15
      SUBPARTITION BY HASH (device_id)
        p2024_03_15_h0  (devices where hash%16==0)
        p2024_03_15_h1
        ...
        p2024_03_15_h15
    p2024_03_16 ...

Query: WHERE device_id=42 AND ts >= '2024-03-15' AND ts < '2024-03-16'
  -> prunes to p2024_03_15 (1 of 365 days)
  -> prunes to p2024_03_15_h10 (1 of 16 sub-parts, hash(42)%16==10)
  -> scans 1/(365*16) = 1/5840 of the table
```

### Q6. You're using Cassandra for a chat app. The query is "latest 50 messages in conversation X, ordered by timestamp." How do you model the partition?
**Answer:** I'd use a table keyed by `conversation_id` as the partition key, with `message_id` (a timeuuid) as the clustering column sorted descending. Schema: `CREATE TABLE messages (conversation_id uuid, message_id timeuuid, sender_id uuid, text text, PRIMARY KEY (conversation_id, message_id)) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (message_id DESC);`. The query becomes `SELECT * FROM messages WHERE conversation_id=? LIMIT 50` — a single-partition read, returning the 50 most recent messages. The partition key `conversation_id` ensures all messages for a conversation are stored together on one node (and its replicas), so the read is one network hop. The clustering column `message_id` (a timeuuid, which sorts by time) means Cassandra stores rows within the partition in time order — the LIMIT 50 returns the latest 50 without scanning. The trade-off: very long conversations (millions of messages) create very large partitions, which can hurt compaction and read latency. Mitigation: bucket conversations by month — `PRIMARY KEY ((conversation_id, bucket_month), message_id)` — so each partition is bounded to one month of messages; fetching the latest 50 hits the current month's partition (and the previous month if fewer than 50 in the current). Real-world: WhatsApp and Discord use this pattern — `conversation_id` as partition key, time-ordered clustering. The Cassandra rule of thumb: keep partitions under 100MB; bucket if needed. For group chats with many members, write fan-out is the bottleneck — each message is one write to the conversation partition, but read status updates are per-member (separate table keyed by member_id).
**Visual:**
```
CREATE TABLE messages (
  conversation_id uuid,        -- PARTITION KEY
  message_id      timeuuid,    -- clustering, DESC
  sender_id       uuid,
  text            text,
  PRIMARY KEY (conversation_id, message_id)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (message_id DESC);

Storage (one partition, all conv_42 messages):
  conv_42 | msg_5 (latest)  -> row 1
  conv_42 | msg_4           -> row 2
  conv_42 | msg_3           -> row 3
  ...

Query: SELECT * FROM messages WHERE conversation_id=42 LIMIT 50
  -> 1 partition, returns latest 50, sub-ms
```

### Q7. You have a PostgreSQL table with 10 years of data (5TB) and ad-hoc analytics queries that filter by various columns (not just date). Partitioning helps how?
**Answer:** For ad-hoc analytics with diverse filters, partitioning by date helps but only partially. The benefit: partition pruning when queries DO filter by date (common in analytics — "last quarter", "year-over-year"). A query `SELECT sum(revenue) FROM sales WHERE sale_date >= '2024-01-01' AND region='EU'` prunes to 2024 partitions, then scans each partition's local index on `region`. Without partitioning, the same query scans a global index covering 10 years — much larger working set, more cache misses. The limitation: a query without a date filter (`SELECT sum(revenue) FROM sales WHERE region='EU'`) hits all partitions — no pruning benefit. For this case, partitioning helps via **parallelism**: PostgreSQL can scan partitions in parallel across CPU cores, giving a 4-8x speedup on multi-core machines. But for true ad-hoc analytics on 5TB, the right answer is usually a **columnar OLAP database** — BigQuery, Snowflake, Redshift, ClickHouse. Columnar stores read only the columns referenced (10x compression, 10x scan speed), and they're designed for full-table scans with predicate pushdown. The hybrid pattern: keep PostgreSQL for OLTP (recent data, point queries, transactions), replicate to a columnar warehouse via CDC for analytics. The warehouse handles ad-hoc queries; PostgreSQL handles transactions. Partitioning the warehouse by date still helps (partition pruning on date filters), but the columnar format is the bigger win. Real-world: Netflix uses PostgreSQL/Cassandra for OLTP and Redshift/Snowflake for analytics; the OLTP database is partitioned for retention, the warehouse is partitioned for query speed.
**Visual:**
```
PostgreSQL (OLTP, partitioned by date):
  -> date-filtered queries: prune to 1 partition, fast
  -> non-date queries: parallel scan across partitions, OK
  -> good for: point lookups, transactions, recent data

Columnar warehouse (OLAP, partitioned by date):
  -> all queries: columnar scan (10x compression)
  -> date-filtered: prune + columnar (100x faster than PG)
  -> good for: ad-hoc analytics, aggregations, full-table scans
```
